summary:
Outpost Horizon is an interactive browser-based mission trainer that lets young players (ages 7–12) manage a Martian outpost in Jezero Crater. As junior astronauts helping Commander Maya, players must balance solar power, oxygen generation, food production, radiation shielding, and the realistic 14-minute light-time communications delay to Earth.

Every Sol presents authentic trade-offs driven by real NASA open data: live and archived solar-flare and radiation risk from DONKI/NOAA, surface weather and dust opacity from Perseverance MEDA, oxygen-production insights from MOXIE, and astronaut-health context from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). Players allocate limited power across life-support modules, respond to dilemmas (solar storms, airlock leaks, dust storms), and experience the consequences of their choices over a multi-Sol mission.

The experience combines a narrative story, 3D outpost visualization, real-time resource simulation, and radio voiceover so children feel the real engineering and operational pressures of deep-space exploration. By turning NASA data into tangible decisions, Outpost Horizon makes the complexities of lunar and Martian outpost operations accessible, educational, and fun.
details:
What it does / How it works

Outpost Horizon is a narrative-driven resource-management game set on a Mars outpost in Jezero Crater. Players take the role of junior astronauts supporting Commander Maya. Each Sol they:

• See a weather forecast and radiation risk derived from real NASA data

• Allocate limited solar power across four modules (O₂ Dome, Farm Dome, Radiation Shield, Rover Lab)

• Face a story dilemma that forces a meaningful trade-off

• Experience the outcome, resource changes, and science takeaway

• Live through realistic light-time communications delays when contacting Earth

The simulation runs for multiple Sols. Resource levels (power, oxygen, food, crew health, science) rise and fall based on player decisions and environmental conditions. Failure occurs if any critical resource reaches zero; success is surviving until the final Sol with a healthy crew and scientific progress.

Benefits & Intended Impact

• Teaches real engineering trade-offs that astronauts and mission planners face

• Makes abstract concepts (radiation shielding, light-time delay, dust opacity, in-situ resource utilization) concrete and memorable for ages 7–12

• Grounds every mechanic in actual NASA open data so players learn authentic science

• Encourages systems thinking, prioritization under uncertainty, and autonomous decision-making

Tools, Languages & Software

• Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (3D outpost visualization)

• Animation: Motion library

• Backend: Express + tsx (Node)

• AI: Google Gemini (text-to-speech for mission radio voiceover)

• Data sources: NASA DONKI, Perseverance MEDA / MOXIE, OSDR, LRO Diviner, NOAA SWPC

• Development: Built and hosted via Google AI Studio template + local development

Creativity

• Combines real-time NASA data feeds with a story-driven game loop and kid-friendly science glossary

• Models the 14-minute Mars–Earth light-time delay as an actual gameplay constraint (players must act before Earth can answer)

• Uses live solar-flare data to dynamically raise radiation risk, forcing players to re-prioritize power and shielding

• 3D visual feedback and radio voiceover create immersion without requiring complex controls

Key design considerations

• Age-appropriate language and short decision cycles so 7–12-year-olds stay engaged

• Every choice has visible, educational consequences

• Fallback to curated NASA archive data when live feeds are unavailable

• Clear visual hierarchy and accessible controls for younger players
